opus-5.5.text:
I think the scope is really the whole story, actually. If you look at the history of automation, most of it has been extremely narrow. You build a machine that does one thing, in one place, under very controlled conditions: a welding robot on a car assembly line, a pick-and-place arm in an electronics factory. Those are enormously valuable, but the economics only work when the task is repeated millions of times in exactly the same way, because all the engineering cost goes into specializing the system for that one job. That's why robots today are concentrated in a handful of industries, and why the vast majority of physical labor in the economy hasn't been touched.

What changes with general-purpose robotic foundation models is that you stop paying that engineering cost per task. If you have a model that has seen a broad range of physical interactions (folding laundry, wiping tables, assembling boxes, handling all kinds of objects), then getting it to do a new task becomes more like prompting or fine-tuning with a modest amount of data, rather than a multi-year integration project. That's analogous to what happened in language. Before large language models, if you wanted a sentiment classifier or a translation system, you built a dedicated pipeline. Now you take a general model and point it at the problem.

So the economic impact comes from the long tail. There are millions of jobs and sub-tasks out there that individually would never justify building a custom robot: restocking shelves in a particular store, cleaning up a particular kitchen, doing some odd step in a small manufacturing shop. Collectively they're a huge fraction of physical work. A generalist system can address that tail, and a specialist system fundamentally can't.

I'd also say that breadth compounds. The more tasks a robot can do, the more places it gets deployed, the more data you collect, and the better and broader it gets. That flywheel is what I think will ultimately determine how fast this goes. It won't come down to one killer application. What matters is whether you can get a system that's good enough at enough things that people actually want to put it out in the world, and then let the deployment itself drive improvement.

Now, I don't want to overstate where we are. Current systems can do some impressive things, but robustness, the ability to handle the hundredth weird situation without failing, is still the hard part. Economically, the threshold isn't "can it do the task once in a demo"; it's "can it do the task reliably enough that it's cheaper and less hassle than the alternative." Once you cross that threshold for a broad enough set of tasks, I think the impact looks less like a new industry and more like a general-purpose technology, something closer to electricity or computing, where it just seeps into everything.

r001.rationale: The response compares general-purpose models with earlier specialized language systems, but it does not discuss incomplete automation of software engineering or attribute it to task-scope limits.

r002.rationale: It discusses robot robustness and reliable performance, but does not identify human oversight for tasks beyond what robots initially handle well.

r003.rationale: It describes robots automating a wider range of work, but does not identify increased productivity of people using robots as a source of economic impact.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually one of the more interesting questions, because I think the way people usually think about it is sort of backwards. The intuition is that you build a robot that does one thing, and then you build a robot that does another thing, and you sort of accumulate economic value one application at a time. And that's how robotics has worked historically. You have a welding robot, you have a palletizing robot, each one is a bespoke engineering effort, and the economics only work out if the task is high-volume and highly repetitive enough to amortize that effort.

But what I think is actually going to happen, and what we're starting to see with foundation models for robotics, is that the scope matters in a very nonlinear way. If you have a robot that can do, say, ten tasks, that's not ten times more valuable than a robot that can do one task. It might be a hundred times more valuable, because the moment a robot can handle the long tail of stuff that comes up in a real environment, you stop needing to engineer the environment around the robot. And that engineering is really where most of the cost is. It's not the robot, it's the fixturing, the integration, the "what happens when something unexpected shows up."

So if you look at a home, or a hospital, or a restaurant kitchen, the reason robots aren't there isn't that any individual task is impossibly hard. Picking up a cup is fine. It's that there are thousands of slightly different things, and the whole value proposition collapses if the robot can only do nine hundred of them and then gets stuck. So I think the economic impact is going to look more like a phase transition than a gradual ramp. For a while it looks like not much is happening, because generalist robots are worse than specialized ones at any particular thing. And then at some point the generality crosses a threshold where it's good enough across the board, and then suddenly a huge number of settings become viable at once.

And the reason I think that's plausible, as opposed to just wishful thinking, is that we already saw exactly this with language models. For a long time, NLP was a bunch of separate systems for separate tasks, and the economics of each one were mediocre. Then you had a single model that was pretty good at all of them, and the economic story changed completely, not because any one capability was amazing, but because of the breadth.

The thing that's different with robots, and the thing I'm honestly less certain about, is the data. With language you had the internet. With robots you have to go out and collect experience in the physical world, and the breadth of the model is going to be bounded by the breadth of that experience. So I think the question of economic impact is really, in disguise, a question about whether we can get the data flywheel going, where deployed robots generate the experience that makes the next generation more capable, which lets you deploy them more widely, and so on. If that loop closes, I think the scope expands very fast. If it doesn't, we're back to the one-application-at-a-time world, and that world is a lot smaller.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robotics and language models, but does not attribute LLMs’ incomplete automation of software engineering to limits in the tasks they perform well.

r002.rationale: It mentions robots getting stuck on unexpected situations, but does not identify human oversight as important for those tasks.

r003.rationale: It describes economic impact through broader robot capability and reduced integration costs, but does not identify increased productivity of people using robots as a source.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is how many different tasks a single robot can do. You can have a robot that is extremely good at one particular task, and that can be economically valuable, but you have to find an application where you’ll do that task enough times to justify the cost of the robot and the engineering required to deploy it.

As the range of capabilities expands, that calculation changes. Imagine a robot that can do a task that takes up only ten minutes of someone’s day. Even if it does that task perfectly, you probably haven’t saved very much. But if it can do a hundred different things that come up throughout the day, now you might have a machine that stays busy and provides a lot of value.

That’s why I think generalization is so important for robotics. It’s not just about having an impressive demonstration of a new skill. It’s about how much additional effort it takes to get the robot to do the next thing. If every new task requires a team of engineers, scaling deployment is going to be difficult. If the robot can learn a new task from a little bit of instruction or experience, then the set of economically viable applications becomes much larger.

Reliability matters enormously too. A broad set of capabilities isn’t enough if a person has to constantly supervise the robot. So I would think about economic impact in terms of both breadth—how much useful work it can do—and autonomy—how much human attention it needs to do that work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robot capabilities and deployment economics, but does not mention LLMs or limits on software engineering automation.

r002.rationale: It says supervision reduces a robot’s value, but does not connect human oversight specifically to tasks beyond those the system initially performs well.

r003.rationale: It describes robots creating value by staying busy and doing useful work, but does not identify increased productivity of people using robots as an economic source.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is how general those capabilities are. We already have robots that are extremely good at particular tasks, and those robots have had a substantial economic impact. But deploying them usually means designing the environment around them. You build a factory so that the robot encounters essentially the same situation over and over again.

If you have a robot that can do a much broader range of things, the economics change. You can put it into an existing environment and have it adapt to the work, instead of adapting the environment to the robot. And you can use the same hardware for different jobs throughout the day.

Think about a robot in a home. Being able to load a dishwasher is useful, but it might not justify buying a robot. If that same robot can also put away groceries, do laundry, tidy up, and help somebody with limited mobility, then the value adds up. So the economic impact isn’t necessarily proportional to how well it does one task. It depends on the breadth of tasks it can perform reliably, and how much effort it takes to get it to perform a new one.

That’s why I’m particularly interested in learning systems that can transfer experience across tasks. If every new application requires a separate engineering project, deployment remains expensive. If teaching a robot something new starts to look more like showing a person how to do a job, then a much larger part of the economy becomes accessible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robots’ task breadth and deployment costs, but does not mention LLMs or software engineering automation.

r002.rationale: It discusses reliability and teaching robots new tasks, but does not identify human oversight as important for tasks beyond robots’ existing capabilities.

r003.rationale: It says robots’ value can add up across tasks, but does not identify increased productivity of people using robots as a source of economic impact.
